the match–mischmatch model is supported in a large sample of newly diagnosed cancer patients, but not in healthy individuals.
newly diagnosed cancer patients who desire more social support than they perceive are at increased risk for anxiety and depressive symptoms.

(1) the hypothesized match-mismatch model is supported in cancer patients but not in healthy controls, (2) the match-mismatch model suggests that lack of social is associated with emotional distress only when patients desire more social support than they actually have, and (3) perceived as well as desired support are relevant and non-overlaping constructs to be included when assessing social support.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question how social support influences emotional distress in cancer patients.
the question whether a mismatch of desired and perceived social support is associated with emotional distress in cancer patients.
the role of social support in the context of cancer and mental health.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a low match (low desired and low perceived support) is associated with a high level of distress, whereas a high mismatch is associated with a low level of distress.
perceived social support is a buffer against emotional distress only if patients desire social support.
a mismatch between desired and perceived social support may be associated with emotional distress.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a mismatch of desired versus perceived support may be an indicator of emotional distress in cancer patients.

perceived support is the key factor in determining the level of emotional distress, but desired support is the key to understanding why some individuals are distressed even though they have high levels of perceived support.
the match–mismath model is relevant for newly diagnosed cancer patients but not for healthy controls.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is important to assess not only the level of support patients actually receive from their social networks, but also their desired support.
it is important to assess both perceived and desired support in order to identify patients at risk of emotional distress.
it is not enough to ask patients whether they have social support, but we need to also ask whether they desire it.
